_comment: THE RECIPE BOOK (docs/plan_crafting_and_materials.md section 3). ONE STRUCTURE: inputs -> outputs, both lists of THINGS, where a thing is a material or a piece of equipment. An alloy, a sled and a loom are the same record with different rows - bronze is not a special case and neither is a tool. A RECIPE READS ONE CHARACTERISTIC (`reads`), and that is what makes 'there is no best hide' real: the sled reads toughness and the hurdles read suppleness, so a mammoth pelt makes an excellent sled and poor halters and a hare pelt does the reverse. Spending the wrong hide on the wrong thing is a mistake the player is free to make. PLAYTEST DIALS.
_comment_work_and_costs: `work` IS WORKER-TURNS FOR ONE OUTPUT PASS, at progress_per_worker_turn x a rate of 1.0. The bench accrues workers x progress_per_worker_turn x craft_speed, and craft_speed is the bounding tool's equipped value or - with no tool - the MATERIAL's own hand_working.rate, which is 0.5 on all three organics and would be 0 for something that cannot be worked bare-handed at all. THAT ZERO IS THE WHOLE REFUSAL MECHANISM: there is no 'you cannot craft that' branch anywhere in the sim, exactly as max(0, attack - defense) refuses a hunt. THE COSTS ARE SIZED SO MATERIAL, NOT BENCH TIME, IS WHAT BINDS. Against the shipped ~17-worker band (equipment.md's kit clock): a gathering half of ~8.5 reaches ~68 biomass a turn, so reeds at 0.02 fibre/biomass pay ~1.4 fibre a turn; a hunting half on Red Deer hauls ~45 biomass, paying ~0.6 hide, ~0.09 bone and ~0.04 fibre. So 6 hide is ~10 turns of banked hide and 5 fibre is ~4 turns of banked fibre, while a 4-hand bench works a `work: 8` sled off in 4 turns bare-handed. BONE IS THE SCARCE ONE BY AN ORDER OF MAGNITUDE (0.0012-0.003 per biomass against hide's 0.006-0.022), so nothing costs more than 3 of it, and that scarcity is what makes Bone-working the slow craft with no dial saying so. AGAINST THE ~15-20 TURN KIT CLOCK (the whole band on that one job, not the half that banks the material): baskets run dry in ~18.5 turns and cost ~4 turns of fibre plus ~2 of hide to replace, so a band keeps its kit alive on roughly a quarter of its material income and spends the rest on tools and stock. Spears last ~42 turns and cost 1 bone, which is ~11 turns of hunting - comfortable. HOES ARE IN-FAMILY RATHER THAN DERIVED: a bone blade hafted with fibre is the same shape as spears and clubs, and `work: 5` sits between clubs (4) and spears (6) - the first build tool the plant web has ever had, so there is no predecessor number to invert. It ships UNGRADED, deliberately, so plant and animal build gear stay consistent until both gain grades together (issue #561). TOOLS ARE THE INVESTMENT: a tanning frame is 8 fibre + 2 bone, ~28 turns of banked material, and it then pays for itself over the 25 items it lasts.
_comment_knowledge: KNOWLEDGE GATES A RECIPE ONLY WHEN THE RECIPE SAYS SO. `requires_knowledge` is absent on every ordinary kit recipe - you can make a sled by hand on turn one, and DOING IT is what teaches Tanning. Every TOOL recipe carries one entry per material it is made from, and validate enforces exactly that: a named craft must be the craft of one of this recipe's own INPUT materials. Paired with the rule that a tool is never made from the material it bounds, that makes the deadlock UNREPRESENTABLE rather than merely avoided - metal needing a crucible that needs metalworking cannot be written down here. TOOLS ARE EARNED, NEVER A PREREQUISITE: there is no opening move where everyone builds tools first, and a tool run dry drops the band back to the rate the game already ships at rather than into a spiral. THE LESSON IS THE RECIPE'S OWN `craft`, charged per ITEM COMPLETED on the same quantum as the tool's wear (intensification_ladder.json's `knowledge.craft_lesson_per_item`, in PRACTICE UNITS, against that craft's own `knowledge.lesson_costs` entry - the same currency and the same divisor a rung's lesson goes through, one quantum over), so what is being made decides what is learned.
_comment_grades: ONE QUALITY LADDER FOR THE WHOLE GAME - THE GRADES ARE THE BANDS. A grade is named by a `characteristic_bands` rung and a recipe declares NO seams of its own: the output's grade is the band of min(material reading, tool quality ceiling), resolved through the same table that rates the hide it was made from. The same four words rate the hide on the panel's rail and the sled you make out of it, so a reading of .55 is `good` in both places. An earlier cut invented coarse/standard/fine, which was a SECOND VOCABULARY FOR ONE IDEA - the player learned quality twice - and, worse, a second set of cut points free to drift from the bands beside them. CONTINUOUS IN, DISCRETE OUT: the reading never scales a resolved stat, it SELECTS a band, and the band declares ABSOLUTES (EquipmentEffect names the value a stat TAKES and has no representation for a multiplier stacking on something else, which is what keeps 'flat until expiry, then a step down' structural rather than remembered). A BAND A RECIPE DOES NOT DECLARE INHERITS THE ONE BELOW IT, so a recipe wanting three steps writes three - and validate rejects a grade key that is not a band, and a lowest grade that is not the FIRST band, because nothing would then answer for a reading of 0.0. THE ANCHOR IS DERIVED, NOT NAMED: it is the band the bench material's bare-handed hand_working.quality_ceiling falls in (0.60 on all three organics, which is `good`), and the grade resolved there must equal the output item's default tier - so a BARE-HANDED CRAFT OFF THE BEST MATERIAL A BAND CAN WORK BY HAND REPRODUCES THE SHIPPED ITEM EXACTLY, and a tool run dry drops the band back to the rate the game already ships at rather than into a spiral. The four rungs fan around that anchor at poor x0.75 / fair x0.85 / good x1.00 / excellent x1.15 - the design's own sled example, 30/34/40/46 on a shipped 40. A GRADE MAY ONLY DECLARE A STAT THE OUTPUT ITEM'S TIERS DECLARE, and must restate that effect's mass bounds verbatim: a grade REPLACES a number rather than adding one, and an excellent snare that dropped `max_body_mass` would quietly become a mammoth trap. A recipe with NO `grades` block says its payload is not tier-bought at all (hurdles' `pen_carry`, the hoes' `build_work`, the wayfinding gear's vantage, a bench tool's craft stats) - the batch is still STAMPED with the band it was made at, that band simply buys it no stat.
_comment_craft_is_derived: `craft` IS THE CRAFT OF THE MATERIAL THE RECIPE READS, and validate rejects any other value. It is written out because that is where a reader needs it, not because it is a second decision - one home per fact, guarded. That is also what keeps the whole model free of a 'primary material' field: the material the recipe READS is the material the bench works, whose tool is consulted, whose bare-handed rate applies and whose craft is practised.
_comment_reads_pairs: THE AXIS PAIRS ARE THE POINT, NOT THE ROWS. Each material's two axes are split between two recipes that want opposite ends, so no source is the upgrade: HIDE - the sled reads `toughness` (a drag harness wants a hide that will not tear) and the hurdles read `suppleness` (halters, a butchering hide, vessels), so a Thunder Mammoth (tough 0.92 / supple 0.10) makes an excellent sled and poor halters and a Snow Hare (0.14 / 0.92) does the exact reverse. FIBRE - baskets read `fineness` (a close weave holds small loose things) and traps read `strength` (a snare is a cord that has to hold), so Cotton (fine 0.92 / strong 0.35) makes excellent baskets and fair snares while Mesquite bast (0.30 / 0.70) is the other way; Flax (0.88 / 0.80) is good at both, which is why it is worth sowing. BONE - spears and clubs read `density` (how well it holds a point, how hard it hits) and wayfinding gear reads `length` (a tally stave needs a long piece), so a Thunder Mammoth tusk (dense 0.88 / long 0.95) is excellent for either while a Rabbit Warren's (0.28 / 0.06) is barely a piece at all.
_comment_tools: THE THREE BENCH TOOLS, AND THE TWO RULES THEY EXIST TO DEMONSTRATE. (1) A MATERIAL'S TOOL IS NEVER MADE FROM THAT MATERIAL: the tanning frame is fibre and bone, the loom is bone and hide, the bone awl is fibre and hide. Otherwise you would need the scarce material to make the thing that stretches it, which is the opposite of what a tool is for. (2) A TOOL IS GATED ON THE CRAFTS OF WHAT IT IS MADE FROM, NEVER ON THE CRAFT IT UNLOCKS - the tanning frame needs Weaving and Bone-working (its two materials) and pointedly NOT Tanning (the craft it serves). Otherwise metal needs a crucible, the crucible needs metalworking, and nothing can start. Both rules are enforced by validate, and together they make the deadlock unwriteable. THE LADDER THEN FALLS OUT WITH NOTHING ADDED: weave baskets bare-handed -> learn Weaving -> knap spears bare-handed -> learn Bone-working -> build a tanning frame -> hide work gets faster, cheaper and can reach `excellent` -> and the same shape repeats the day clay and metal have producers. WHAT EACH TOOL BUYS is on the item in equipment.json, beside its durability.
